title: The Hottest New Side Hustle Is Stripping Copper Wire and Posting About It
gist: Wired profiles a TikTok niche of copper-wire strippers, showing that creators mostly earn from views and TikTok Shop affiliate sales rather than scrap itself. Copper hit a record of about $14,473 per metric ton in September, more than double its price in September 2020.

insights.claim: Copper reached an all-time high this year; per IMF data it was worth about $14,473 per metric ton ($7.23 per pound) in September, more than double September 2020.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: The record price is the trigger making scrapping attractive to amateurs.
insights.locator: Selling scrap copper is nothing new

insights.claim: Economist Craig Depken II says copper theft tends to rise when copper prices rise and when economic distress is high enough that people judge the payoff outweighs the risk of being caught.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Rising copper plus household stress is a combination that predicts more scrapping and theft.

insights.claim: There is no reliable data on how often people sell scrap copper, so theft rates are used as a proxy for scrapping activity.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Informal-economy demand for metals is poorly measured.

themes.theme: Creator economics: the content pays, not the metal

insights.claim: A creator saving $20,000 for a home earned just $99 from 30 pounds of copper stripped over six months; one TikTok video with 6.8 million views earned $1,446, so most of the money came from the platform.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: The scrap is the content prop, and platform payouts are the actual income.
insights.quote: earned just $99 selling 30 pounds of copper stripped over six months

insights.claim: King of Copper claimed about $90 of metal from five hours of stripping and melting, and $47 of copper from two hours dismantling a 110-pound air conditioner, which implies hourly returns of roughly $18 and $23.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Scrapping returns are low and only make sense as a side hustle or content source.

insights.claim: Creators can earn commissions marketing wire strippers on TikTok Shop; the most popular stripper has sold more than 20,000 units globally, and one affiliate says 5-10 a day sell and it is his biggest seller.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Selling picks and shovels through affiliate links is the clearest monetization in this niche.
insights.quote: It's been my biggest seller since l started doing affiliate videos.

insights.claim: AI-generated ads with synthetic imagery and voice-overs, some using near-identical scripts promising 'eight grand a week' from scrap copper, compete with human sellers even in the niche wire-stripper market.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Low-cost AI ads can saturate even small niches and push claims that are likely exaggerated.

insights.claim: Scholar Benjamin Stickle sorts legal scrappers into three groups: people making ends meet, workers selling scrap they get on the job, and people raising money for charity.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Stickle
insights.so_what: Creator-influencers blur these categories since they also earn from the platform.
insights.locator: Benjamin Stickle, a criminal justice professor

insights.claim: Selling lawfully obtained scrap copper is legal across the US except Minnesota, which requires a state-issued license, and insulated wire sells for a fraction of stripped copper, which pushes resellers to strip it themselves.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: The price gap between insulated and stripped copper explains the demand for strippers.
insights.locator: The final price of recycled copper

insights.claim: Offline, scrappers often operate in small teams, split profits, and donate metal to those experiencing homelessness, a community that is not visible on TikTok.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Stickle
insights.so_what: Informal mutual aid underlies a trade that appears solitary online.
